clue.text: Notice evidence of measles?

definitions.meaning: a verb here: to catch sight of
one of the red marks the illness leaves on the skin

explanation.surface: A worried parent looking for signs of a childhood illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notice' looks like a noun, a sign on a wall; it is the verb. The question mark flags that one red mark is only a single piece of the evidence.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain verb synonym for catching sight of something, and also the noun for each red blemish of a measles rash.

clue.text: Manufactured item supporting pipe

parts.note: a duct is a pipe or channel

explanation.surface: A factory component that holds up a pipe, like a bracket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporting pipe' reads as one phrase describing the item; it splits into two pieces instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Whatever a factory turns out and sells is its output, the general word for goods made by industry.

clue.text: Minor change that's initially not very effective?

indicators.note: at the start, so only the first letter of the word before it counts

explanation.surface: A remark that a small adjustment won't achieve much at first.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the joke: a small adjustment is by nature not very effective, so the wordplay describes the answer too.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal word for a small fine adjustment, as when an engineer adjusts settings slightly.

clue.text: Briars to upset tree specialist

indicators.note: to upset is to knock over and throw into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Thorny bushes annoying the person who looks after the trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' looks like part of the infinitive 'to upset', but its letters are fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: From Latin arbor, 'tree': a professional who prunes, fells and cares for woody plants.

clue.text: Trouble beginning to affect party

indicators.note: the beginning of the next word is its first letter

parts.note: informal British word for a social gathering

explanation.surface: Disruption starting to spoil a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'do' is British slang for a party, as in 'a birthday do'.
explanation.definitionFit: Means fuss or bother, familiar from the phrases 'much ado about nothing' and 'without further ado'.

clue.text: Embargoes limiting movement of money? Not at all

indicators.note: limiting means hemming in, so the embargoes word goes round the other letters
movement of the money means its letters are moved about into a new order

explanation.surface: Trade embargoes restrict the flow of capital; the speaker says this isn't happening at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'movement of' rearranges MONEY into YNOME, which BANS is 'limiting', giving B-YNOME-ANS.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is an emphatic negative, used exactly where one might say certainly not or in no way.

clue.text: Come back to minister, one with seat

parts.note: to seat oneself is to sit

explanation.surface: Returning to see a churchman, one who holds a parliamentary seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seat' reads as a noun, a chair or a constituency; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally visiting a place again, and figuratively returning to reconsider an old question or decision.

clue.text: American aboard vessel cut down oriental food

indicators.note: on board a ship means inside it

parts.note: SHIP without its final P; S…HI goes around the rest

explanation.surface: A US passenger on a small boat eating an Asian dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut down' suggests a smaller vessel; it only trims the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Japanese dish of vinegared rice with raw fish, so an example of East Asian cuisine.

clue.text: Leaders in Home Office intend to hold line over purchase arrangement

indicators.note: leaders are the front letters, here of each of the words Home and Office

parts.note: the opening letters of Home and Office

indicators.note: to hold means to contain, so the intend word wraps round the other letters

parts.note: O is the cricket scorebook abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Government officials plan to keep a policy line on how buyers finance purchases.
explanation.walkthrough: HO comes from the leaders of Home Office; MEAN is used 'to hold' L and O, giving ME-LO-AN.
explanation.definitionFit: A mortgage is a loan arranged to finance buying a house, so it is literally an arrangement for a purchase.

clue.text: Former soldier retaining second garment

indicators.note: to retain is to keep hold of, so the outer word keeps the letter inside it

explanation.surface: An ex-serviceman keeping a spare piece of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' reads as 'spare' or 'another'; it is just the abbreviation S.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain an undershirt, in North America a waistcoat; either way a specific piece of clothing.

clue.text: Get rid of boat in Asia

definitions.meaning: a flat-bottomed Chinese sailing ship with battened sails

explanation.surface: Disposing of a vessel somewhere in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface runs the two senses together as one act, scrapping a boat; they are two separate meanings of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal verb for discarding rubbish, and the name of the traditional Chinese sailing vessel.

clue.text: Feature of St Paul's criticism, mainly of the family

parts.note: St Paul's Cathedral in London is famous for its dome

explanation.surface: Commentary on a London cathedral's features, mostly about its family history.
explanation.walkthrough: Stick in the sense of criticism is British informal, as in 'getting stick from the fans'.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to home and household life, as in domestic chores or a domestic dispute between relatives.

clue.text: One setting off to read, not fidgeting

indicators.note: restless shifting about, so the letters will not keep still in their order

explanation.surface: Someone settling down to read quietly without fidgeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not fidgeting' reads as sitting still, but 'not' is fodder and 'fidgeting' alone is the indicator; 'setting off' means igniting, not departing.
explanation.definitionFit: The device that triggers an explosive charge, so the thing that sets off a bomb.

clue.text: Austere saint welcomes joke for the most part

indicators.note: a host welcomes guests in, so the outer word takes the other inside

explanation.surface: A severe holy figure who nonetheless enjoys a good joke.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface contrast, a stern saint who likes a laugh, hides that 'welcomes' is only a container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe severe, unindulgent discipline; a stern regime or rules without leniency.

clue.text: Top prize money for session of cricket

indicators.note: to top is to cut off the head, so the first letter of the word is removed

parts.note: winnings are money won as a prize

explanation.surface: A phrase naming the largest prize payout awarded for a period of cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' is a verb here, not an adjective: it beheads WINNINGS, removing W.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket an innings is a team's or batter's turn at batting, a distinct period of play.

clue.text: A second pupil, not entirely perceptive

explanation.surface: Describing a runner-up student who is only partly sharp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not entirely perceptive' reads as a verdict on the pupil; 'not entirely' belongs to the pupil and 'perceptive' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrewd and quick to see how things really are, a near synonym for sharp-witted insight.

clue.text: Someone scolding in manner carried weight

indicators.note: the first part is put in the second

parts.note: tone = manner of speaking; TON…E goes around
a nag is a person who scolds

explanation.surface: A telling-off whose manner of delivery carried real weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carried weight' reads as 'was influential'; here it is a noun phrase, the load a ship carries.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's cargo capacity or the total load it transports, measured in tons.

clue.text: Pay ranges in shifts

indicators.note: to shift is to move position, so the letters change places

explanation.surface: Wages vary depending on which work shifts you do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shifts' looks like work shifts, which suits 'pay'; it is the rearrangement signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Money received for work, so a plain noun synonym for wages or salary.

clue.text: Main star appearing in surreal phantasy

indicators.note: the answer makes an appearance inside the words that follow

parts.note: the last two letters of 'surreal' run on into the first three of 'phantasy'

explanation.surface: The lead actor of a dreamlike fantasy film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main star' suggests a lead actor; it means the brightest star in a constellation.
explanation.definitionFit: Astronomers label the brightest star of a constellation with the first Greek letter, as in Alpha Centauri.

clue.text: Book on Dalton's debut as film spy

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so only the opening letter of Dalton is used

parts.note: the name Dalton, which supplies its opening letter

explanation.surface: A reference to Timothy Dalton's first outing playing the famous secret agent on screen.
explanation.walkthrough: Timothy Dalton played this spy in two films, so the surface reads naturally while 'debut' just gives D.
explanation.definitionFit: James Bond is Ian Fleming's secret agent, hero of a long-running cinema franchise.

clue.text: New baby? Husband and family mostly bowled over

indicators.note: bowled over means knocked down and turned upside down, so in a down entry the letters run in reverse

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for husband in genealogy and listings

indicators.note: mostly means all but the final letter of the family word is used

parts.note: a tribe is a family group or clan

explanation.surface: A husband and his relatives are overwhelmed with joy at the arrival of a new baby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts TRIBE to TRIB; H plus TRIB is HTRIB, which 'bowled over' turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: A birth is the arrival of a child, so a new baby is an example of one, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Present favourable impression of quick trip

definitions.meaning: what a press officer does to a story, slanting it
a short drive for pleasure, as in 'a ride out in the car'

explanation.surface: A press officer talking up a short journey.
explanation.walkthrough: The PR sense is the modern 'spin doctor' one; the trip sense is the older British 'go for a spin in the car'.
explanation.definitionFit: Political slang for slanting news favourably, and informal for a brief pleasure drive.

clue.text: Leaves drinker finally imprisoned by magistrate for drinking session

parts.note: tea is sold as dried leaves

indicators.note: imprisoned by means held inside, so the magistrate word encloses the other letter

parts.note: beak is British slang for a magistrate or judge

indicators.note: finally points to only the last letter of drinker

parts.note: the word drinker, which supplies its last letter

explanation.surface: A heavy drinker finally leaves after being locked up by a magistrate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb but is the noun, tea leaves. R ('finally' in drinker) is 'imprisoned by' BEAK, giving BREAK.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea break is a short pause at work for a cuppa, a session spent drinking tea.

clue.text: Skill in stage role (not lead)

indicators.note: not lead means without its leading letter, so the opening letter of the role word is dropped

parts.note: an actor's role on stage is a part

explanation.surface: Real skill shows in playing a supporting stage role rather than the lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not lead' suggests a minor role, but it removes the first letter, P, from PART.
explanation.definitionFit: Art can mean a craft or technique, as in the art of conversation, so it is a synonym for skill.

clue.text: Various arts with inks revealing ancient script

indicators.note: varied, so the letters come in a different order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters; 'with' joins the two words

explanation.surface: Calligraphy techniques used to decipher an old manuscript.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all penmanship, arts and inks, which fits the definition; 'with' only strings the two fodder words together.
explanation.definitionFit: Classical language of India, written in Devanagari, in which the Vedas were composed.

clue.text: That chap backed the French scoundrel

indicators.note: moved backwards, as a car is backed out, so the letters run in reverse

explanation.surface: A man who supported the French turns out to be a villain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed' reads as 'supported'; it turns LE round.
explanation.definitionFit: Dated slang for a cad or contemptible man, someone who behaves dishonourably.
